did_you_know.text: Did you know? David noticed the contrast between the cedar house where he lived and the Ark of the LORD, which was kept under curtains. He therefore told Nathan the prophet that he wanted to build a house for the LORD.
Did you know? The prophet Nathan initially approved David’s desire, but that same night he received the word of the LORD, which made clear that he had to deliver a different message to David.
Did you know? The LORD emphasizes that He had not lived in a permanent house since bringing Israel out of Egypt. Instead, He had moved from tent to tent and from tabernacle to tabernacle.
Did you know? The LORD reminds David of the beginning of his journey: He took him from the pasture and from following the sheep and appointed him ruler over Israel.
Did you know? Along with choosing David, the LORD describes how He accompanied and protected him: He was with him, defeated his enemies, and promised to make his name great.

Did you know? This chapter contains a play on the meaning of the word “house”: David wanted to build a house for the LORD, but the LORD announced that He would build David a “house”—a lasting dynasty and kingdom.

Did you know? According to the LORD’s promise, David’s offspring would rise after him, and he would be the one to build the house for the LORD. This distinguishes David’s mission from that of his successor.

Did you know? The relationship between the LORD and David’s successor is described in the language of father and son: “I will be his father, and he will be my son,” along with the promise that the LORD’s steadfast love would not be withdrawn from him.
Did you know? After hearing the prophecy, David went in and sat before the LORD. His prayer begins with humility: “Who am I, Lord GOD, and what is my family, that you have brought me this far?”
Did you know? David praises Israel as “one nation on earth” and recalls that the LORD redeemed a people for Himself so that they would be His people forever and so that He would be their God.
